mapping_rows.old_stance: Do not treat all representative bodies as equivalent; the source contrasts nominated assemblies under royal control with historically grounded estates possessing broader constituencies and bargaining power.
successor_labels: Provincial assemblies and demands for provincial estates

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Economic liberalization in Calonne's reform program» as explicitly named facet(s) under Economic liberalization in Calonne's reform program. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Economic liberalization in Calonne's reform program
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The program revived Physiocratic measures associated with Turgot by freeing the grain trade, removing internal customs barriers, and converting the corvee into a tax to stimulate prosperity and revenue.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat these as economic components of a larger fiscal strategy, not as the immediate cause of the political confrontation; several passed registration with little resistance.
successor_labels: Economic liberalization in Calonne's reform program

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Representative consent and authority to tax» as explicitly named facet(s) under Estates-General: emergence as the demanded constitutional remedy. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Representative consent and authority to tax
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The central constitutional issue became which body could legitimately authorize permanent or new taxation and on what financial evidence such consent should rest.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Distinguish consultation, advice, registration, and national consent; the Notables and parlements did not claim identical representative authority, and many explicitly denied their own competence to grant taxes.
successor_labels: Estates-General: emergence as the demanded constitutional remedy

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Financial transparency, accounts, and independent audit» as explicitly named facet(s) under Assembly of Notables—reform consent, financial scrutiny and the audit dispute. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Financial transparency, accounts, and independent audit
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Competing claims about surplus and deficit made full accounts, plans of economy, and independent verification prerequisites for consent and credit.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Present demands for transparency as substantively grounded as well as politically useful; the king's refusal of permanent audit reflected concern for royal prerogative.
successor_labels: Assembly of Notables—reform consent, financial scrutiny and the audit dispute

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «The Notables' qualified support for reform» as explicitly named facet(s) under Assembly of Notables—reform consent, financial scrutiny and the audit dispute. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: The Notables' qualified support for reform
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Most Notables favored many reform principles, including tax equality and taxpayer representation, while objecting to the land tax's design, institutional safeguards, clerical provisions, insufficient accounts, and their own uncertain authority.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Reject a simple interpretation that privileged Notables opposed reform as such; the source attributes failure to distrust, design objections, representational limits, and institutional interests.
successor_labels: Assembly of Notables—reform consent, financial scrutiny and the audit dispute

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Clerical debt and the clergy's right of self-taxation» as explicitly named facet(s) under Territorial subvention and equality of taxation. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Clerical debt and the clergy's right of self-taxation
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Plans to redeem the clergy's corporate debt threatened the institutional basis of its traditional self-taxation, leading bishops to insist that only the Assembly of the Clergy could consent.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Frame the objection as defense of corporate fiscal autonomy, not simply refusal by clergy to contribute anything.
successor_labels: Territorial subvention and equality of taxation

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Calonne's Avertissement and failed appeal to public opinion» as explicitly named facet(s) under Calonne's borrowing, spending, loss of confidence, and dismissal. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Calonne's Avertissement and failed appeal to public opinion
mapping_rows.old_meaning: After losing control of the Notables in private, Calonne published his proposals and portrayed resistance as privileged self-interest, attempting to mobilize public pressure behind reform.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The source treats this as a bold but politically disastrous maneuver: its egalitarian language did not overcome Calonne's loss of credibility and instead helped politicize the conflict.
successor_labels: Calonne's borrowing, spending, loss of confidence, and dismissal

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Brienne's ministry and reform strategy» as explicitly named facet(s) under Brienne's ministry and five-year financial recovery plan. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Brienne's ministry and reform strategy
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Brienne inherited Calonne's fiscal program, modified taxes and representative institutions, negotiated with the parlements, proposed a five-year recovery, and finally backed a judicial reconstruction before credit collapsed.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Do not reduce Brienne to passive failure; he repeatedly adapted policy and initially restored credit, but optimism, reversals, coercion, and dependence on borrowing could not overcome the combined political and fiscal crisis.
preserved_access: Lomenie de Brienne--financial and judicial reforms
successor_labels: Brienne's ministry and five-year financial recovery plan

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Brienne's five-year financial recovery plan and the Troyes compromise» as explicitly named facet(s) under Brienne's ministry and five-year financial recovery plan. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Brienne's five-year financial recovery plan and the Troyes compromise
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Brienne withdrew the stamp and land taxes, prolonged existing vingtiemes on a more equitable basis, promised accounts and economies, recalled the Paris Parlement, and planned loans to restore finances by 1792.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat the compromise as tactically successful but politically costly: it ended the exile and bought time while appearing to betray the principle that only the Estates-General could authorize taxation.
successor_labels: Brienne's ministry and five-year financial recovery plan

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Lamoignon's judicial reform strategy» as explicitly named facet(s) under Lamoignon's Plenary Court and grand bailliage reforms. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Lamoignon's judicial reform strategy
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Lamoignon, appointed to lead the judiciary, favored comprehensive legal reform and ultimately designed the May restructuring intended to remove the parlements' capacity to obstruct royal policy.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Preserve both sides of his program: institutional coercion against the parlements and substantive criminal-law reform presented to enlightened opinion.
successor_labels: Lamoignon's Plenary Court and grand bailliage reforms

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Vergennes's foreign policy and ministerial role» as explicitly named facet(s) under American War of Independence: French intervention and fiscal consequences; Calonne's borrowing, spending, loss of confidence, and dismissal; Dutch crisis of 1787 and French non-intervention. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Vergennes's foreign policy and ministerial role
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Vergennes drove intervention against Britain, supported Calonne within the ministry, and backed the Dutch Patriots; his death and France's later inability to intervene highlighted declining state capacity.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Keep his distinct roles connected but not conflated: American strategy, Calonne's political protection, and Dutch policy each matter to the chapter's account of fiscal and ministerial weakness.
successor_labels: American War of Independence: French intervention and fiscal consequences

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Parlement of Paris as center of opposition» as explicitly named facet(s) under Parlement of Paris: resistance to taxation and royal registration. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Parlement of Paris as center of opposition
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The Parlement of Paris turned demands for accounts and resistance to permanent taxes into a popular constitutional campaign, then opposed forced registration, royal sessions, arbitrary arrest, and judicial reconstruction.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Represent the court as a powerful institutional opponent with genuine constitutional arguments and public backing, while retaining the source's doubts about its representative character and consistency.
successor_labels: Parlement of Paris: resistance to taxation and royal registration

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Registration, remonstrance, and lit de justice» as explicitly named facet(s) under Parlement of Paris: resistance to taxation and royal registration. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Registration, remonstrance, and lit de justice
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The monarchy's laws required registration by sovereign courts, while remonstrances and royal ceremonies of forced registration became the procedural battleground over taxation, legality, and constitutional authority.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Keep the procedures distinct: remonstrance expressed judicial objection, a lit de justice imposed registration, and the novel Royal Session purported to permit free opinion before an order to register.
successor_labels: Parlement of Paris: resistance to taxation and royal registration

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Exile of the Parlement of Paris to Troyes and negotiated return» as explicitly named facet(s) under Parlement of Paris: resistance to taxation and royal registration. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Exile of the Parlement of Paris to Troyes and negotiated return
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The Crown exiled the Parlement after it repudiated forced tax registration, then Brienne recalled it through a compromise that withdrew new taxes and prolonged existing ones.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat the episode as a temporary negotiated settlement whose perceived inconsistency disappointed both public and provincial allies.
successor_labels: Parlement of Paris: resistance to taxation and royal registration

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Dutch Patriot crisis and French inability to intervene» as explicitly named facet(s) under Dutch crisis of 1787 and French non-intervention. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Dutch Patriot crisis and French inability to intervene
mapping_rows.old_meaning: French support for Dutch Patriots confronted a British-backed Prussian intervention, but the fiscal crisis prevented military preparation and forced France to stand aside.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Present the episode as evidence of the interaction between fiscal weakness, foreign-policy incapacity, and loss of governmental prestige, not as an independent cause of the domestic crisis.
successor_labels: Dutch crisis of 1787 and French non-intervention

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Royal Session of 19 November 1787» as explicitly named facet(s) under Royal Session of 19 November 1787 and the rupture over despotism. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Royal Session of 19 November 1787
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Brienne convened an unprecedented session in the king's presence to secure authoritative support for a large loan program, but Louis XVI's order to register after free debate triggered a legality crisis.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Distinguish the apparent majority support for loans from the procedural disaster caused by treating the session like a lit de justice at its conclusion.
successor_labels: Royal Session of 19 November 1787 and the rupture over despotism

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Civil rights for French Protestants» as explicitly named facet(s) under Civil rights for French Protestants. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Civil rights for French Protestants
mapping_rows.old_meaning: An edict granting civil rights to Protestants was introduced to create goodwill at the Royal Session, then delayed as parlementary conflict over despotism intensified.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat the reform as substantively important but also politically staged; do not imply that it caused the loan dispute.
successor_labels: Civil rights for French Protestants

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Duke of Orleans's legality protest and Louis XVI's reply» as explicitly named facet(s) under Duke d'Orléans's protest at the Royal Session. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Duke of Orleans's legality protest and Louis XVI's reply
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Orleans challenged the ordered registration of loans at the Royal Session, and the king's improvised appeal to personal will transformed a near-success into a symbol of arbitrary government.
mapping_rows.old_stance: The significance lies less in Orleans's dynastic identity than in how the exchange crystallized the conflict between royal will and legality.
successor_labels: Duke d'Orléans's protest at the Royal Session

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Lettres de cachet and freedom from arbitrary arrest» as explicitly named facet(s) under Lettres de cachet, arbitrary arrest, and the fundamental laws. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Lettres de cachet and freedom from arbitrary arrest
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Exiles and arrests by royal warrant became a central example of despotism, prompting the parlements to claim freedom from arbitrary arrest as a fundamental right.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Distinguish the specific legal instrument from the broader rhetoric of despotism; the source traces how its use turned procedural conflict into a rights claim.
successor_labels: Lettres de cachet, arbitrary arrest, and the fundamental laws

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Parlementary constitutionalism and the fundamental laws» as explicitly named facet(s) under Lettres de cachet, arbitrary arrest, and the fundamental laws. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Parlementary constitutionalism and the fundamental laws
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The Parlement of Paris formulated a constitutional doctrine combining national consent to taxation, registration of laws, judicial tenure, provincial rights, property, natural judges, and personal liberty.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Present this as the Parlement's articulated view of the constitution, not as a neutral codification accepted by all parties; the Crown answered that judicial claims created an aristocracy of magistrates.
successor_labels: Lettres de cachet, arbitrary arrest, and the fundamental laws

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Maupeou's 1771 judicial precedent» as explicitly named facet(s) under Lamoignon's Plenary Court and grand bailliage reforms. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Maupeou's 1771 judicial precedent
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The 1771 destruction and replacement of the parlements supplied both a strategic model for coercive reform and a warning about political memory, partial bankruptcy, and eventual restoration.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat Maupeou as an operative precedent shaping expectations in 1788, not merely a historical comparison added by the narrator.
successor_labels: Lamoignon's Plenary Court and grand bailliage reforms

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Plenary Court, grand bailliages, and the architecture of the May Edicts» as explicitly named facet(s) under Lamoignon's Plenary Court and grand bailliage reforms. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Plenary Court, grand bailliages, and the architecture of the May Edicts
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The May settlement transferred registration to a new Plenary Court, reduced parlements to appeal functions, expanded forty-seven lower courts, and suppressed offices made redundant by reduced jurisdiction.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Keep each institutional change distinct and relate it to the common purpose of ending parlementary obstruction; do not treat the program solely as an abstract constitutional declaration.
successor_labels: Lamoignon's Plenary Court and grand bailliage reforms

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Criminal-law reform as a companion to the May judicial coup» as explicitly named facet(s) under Criminal-law reform in the May 1788 program. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Criminal-law reform as a companion to the May judicial coup
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The government coupled its attack on parlementary power with reforms addressing abuses and miscarriages of justice in order to appeal to enlightened opinion.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Preserve the reforms' substantive significance while noting their strategic placement; the narrative does not say they were merely insincere window dressing.
successor_labels: Criminal-law reform in the May 1788 program

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Nationwide provincial and social resistance to the May Edicts» as explicitly named facet(s) under Provincial, noble, clerical, and popular revolt in 1788. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Nationwide provincial and social resistance to the May Edicts
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Sovereign and lower courts, bars, local crowds, nobles, clergy, civic groups, and some military officers resisted or obstructed the May settlement across France.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Do not flatten the coalition into a single ideology; actors defended different institutional, corporate, local, and constitutional interests but converged in rejecting ministerial coercion and demanding representative bodies.
successor_labels: Provincial, noble, clerical, and popular revolt in 1788

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Day of Tiles at Grenoble» as explicitly named facet(s) under Day of Tiles at Grenoble. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Day of Tiles at Grenoble
mapping_rows.old_meaning: When officials tried to exile Grenoble's magistrates, urban resistance used rooftop projectiles against troops, causing deaths and injuries and becoming a prominent symbol of provincial revolt.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Index the event as a consequential episode within the wider resistance, not as the sole beginning or cause of national revolt.
successor_labels: Day of Tiles at Grenoble

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Judicial paralysis and lower-court resistance» as explicitly named facet(s) under Provincial, noble, clerical, and popular revolt in 1788. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Judicial paralysis and lower-court resistance
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Lower courts, the Paris bar, reform jurists, and provincial tribunals refused to recognize or cooperate with the new judicial order, bringing ordinary justice close to a standstill.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Preserve the limited exceptions: some lower courts were tempted by promotion, but uncertainty and institutional loyalties prevented broad compliance.
successor_labels: Provincial, noble, clerical, and popular revolt in 1788

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Clerical and noble resistance in 1788» as explicitly named facet(s) under Provincial, noble, clerical, and popular revolt in 1788. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Clerical and noble resistance in 1788
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Unauthorized noble assemblies and the Assembly of the Clergy joined demands for national or provincial Estates and denounced ministerial policy, broadening resistance beyond magistrates and crowds.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Keep noble and clerical motives distinct even when providing a shared route to the cross-estate coalition; neither group should be presented as speaking for all commoners or all France.
successor_labels: Provincial, noble, clerical, and popular revolt in 1788

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Military officers and the limits of coercion» as explicitly named facet(s) under Provincial, noble, clerical, and popular revolt in 1788. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Military officers and the limits of coercion
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Although troops enforced some arrests and registrations, officers whose careers had been harmed by reforms were widely suspected of hostility, and commanders hesitated to use lethal force against rioters.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Do not claim military mutiny: the source explicitly notes that no officer disobeyed a decisive order, while emphasizing reluctance and political unreliability.
successor_labels: Provincial, noble, clerical, and popular revolt in 1788

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «July 1788 hailstorm, harvest damage, and the fiscal shock» as explicitly named facet(s) under Hailstorm of 13 July 1788 as a fiscal shock. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: July 1788 hailstorm, harvest damage, and the fiscal shock
mapping_rows.old_meaning: A destructive hailstorm and wider bad weather reduced expected harvests, made future peasant tax payments doubtful, and further undermined the tax-backed advances on which the treasury depended.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat weather as a proximate aggravating shock, not the underlying cause of bankruptcy; the fiscal system was already weakened by debt, arrears, and political resistance.
successor_labels: Hailstorm of 13 July 1788 as a fiscal shock

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Treasury suspension of payments and financial panic» as explicitly named facet(s) under Bankruptcy and collapse of the Old Regime, August 1788. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Treasury suspension of payments and financial panic
mapping_rows.old_meaning: After further advances became unavailable, the treasury suspended payments, substituted interest-bearing paper, and triggered a fall in government funds, a bank run, and an emergency political response.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Keep the concrete financial events accessible separately from the broader interpretive claim that the old regime collapsed in every sense.
successor_labels: Bankruptcy and collapse of the Old Regime, August 1788

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Lafayette's role in the Assembly of Notables» as explicitly named facet(s) under Lafayette in the Assembly of Notables. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Lafayette's role in the Assembly of Notables
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Lafayette used his position among the Notables to press for accountability and a genuinely national assembly, helping make the Estates-General an explicit political demand.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Preserve the narrative's skepticism about his self-presentation and ambition while recognizing his substantive role in articulating representative demands.
successor_labels: Lafayette in the Assembly of Notables

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Parlement of Bordeaux and the provincial countermodel» as explicitly named facet(s) under Provincial assemblies and demands for provincial estates. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Parlement of Bordeaux and the provincial countermodel
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The Bordeaux court demanded stronger provincial estates, resisted vague assemblies and tax registration, endured exile, and later helped expose the weakness of nominated provincial institutions.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat Bordeaux as a sustained provincial counterpoint to Paris, not merely another instance in a list of courts.
successor_labels: Provincial assemblies and demands for provincial estates

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Pamphleteering, political clubs, and the expanding political public» as explicitly named facet(s) under Public opinion and political pamphleteering in the crisis of 1787-1788. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Pamphleteering, political clubs, and the expanding political public
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Leaks, pamphlets, broadsheets, salons, and clubs circulated fiscal and constitutional arguments, sustained opposition, and widened political participation beyond formal institutions.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Distinguish information networks and organized discussion from the broader category of public opinion; publications varied in accuracy and motive but materially shaped the crisis.
successor_labels: Public opinion and political pamphleteering in the crisis of 1787-1788

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Urban crowds, demonstrations, and popular disorder» as explicitly named facet(s) under Public opinion and political pamphleteering in the crisis of 1787-1788. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Urban crowds, demonstrations, and popular disorder
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Crowds in Paris and provincial cities supported courts, celebrated exiles' returns, challenged police and troops, and sometimes used violence, making street politics part of the institutional crisis.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Do not interpret every crowd as sharing one program; support for magistrates, hostility to ministers, local grievances, employment disruption, and resistance to coercion overlapped.
successor_labels: Public opinion and political pamphleteering in the crisis of 1787-1788

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Centralization of the royal treasury and displacement of private financiers» as explicitly named facet(s) under Brienne's ministry and five-year financial recovery plan. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Centralization of the royal treasury and displacement of private financiers
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Brienne proposed consolidating financial operations in a bureaucratic treasury and reducing private financiers' traditional role, but this made those same financiers less willing to rescue the government when advances failed.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Preserve the double effect: administrative centralization was a reform goal, yet its threatened beneficiaries had little incentive to supply emergency credit.
successor_labels: Brienne's ministry and five-year financial recovery plan

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «D'Epremesnil and militant parlementary leadership» as explicitly named facet(s) under Lettres de cachet, arbitrary arrest, and the fundamental laws. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: D'Epremesnil and militant parlementary leadership
mapping_rows.old_meaning: D'Epremesnil emerged as a leading younger magistrate, pressed for an early Estates-General, formulated the fundamental-laws declaration, and resisted arrest within the Parlement.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat him as a consequential leader within the court rather than making his personal actions stand for the entire Parlement.
successor_labels: Lettres de cachet, arbitrary arrest, and the fundamental laws

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Joly de Fleury's wartime fiscal measures» as explicitly named facet(s) under Joly de Fleury. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Joly de Fleury's wartime fiscal measures
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Necker's immediate successor raised taxes and additional loans to sustain war finance after confidence was weakened by Necker's resignation.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Supplemental access is defensible, but the brief transitional treatment should not be inflated into a separate major reform program.
successor_labels: Joly de Fleury

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Anglo-French commercial treaty of 1786» as explicitly named facet(s) under Economic liberalization in Calonne's reform program. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Anglo-French commercial treaty of 1786
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Vergennes concluded a free-trade agreement with Britain as part of an economic strategy expected to benefit French agriculture.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Within this owned chapter the treaty receives only brief prospective treatment; later economic consequences belong to the next chapter and are not evidence owned here.
successor_labels: Economic liberalization in Calonne's reform program

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Miromesnil's dismissal and replacement» as explicitly named facet(s) under Miromesnil. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Miromesnil's dismissal and replacement
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Louis XVI dismissed his long-serving judicial minister during Calonne's final crisis and replaced him with the reform-minded Lamoignon.
mapping_rows.old_stance: This is useful personnel access but not an independently developed policy analysis; keep it subordinate to ministerial succession and judicial reform.
successor_labels: Miromesnil

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Proceedings against Calonne and his exile» as explicitly named facet(s) under Calonne's borrowing, spending, loss of confidence, and dismissal. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Proceedings against Calonne and his exile
mapping_rows.old_meaning: After Calonne's fall, the Parlement of Paris sought proceedings for misuse of public funds; the government quashed them after he had fled to England.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Treat the allegation and proceeding as political conflict, not as a source-verified finding that Calonne committed the charged offense.
successor_labels: Calonne's borrowing, spending, loss of confidence, and dismissal

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Louis XVI's decisions and loss of governing authority» as explicitly named facet(s) under Louis XVI: prerogative, indecision, and political miscalculation. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Louis XVI's decisions and loss of governing authority
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Louis XVI authorized war and successive reform strategies, protected and dismissed ministers, defended royal prerogative, imposed registrations and judicial changes, and ultimately accepted the Estates-General when credit and authority failed.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Avoid both a passive-king account and an all-controlling one: the source repeatedly shows consequential royal choices, hesitation, personal dislikes, procedural mistakes, and dependence on ministers and public credit.
successor_labels: Louis XVI: prerogative, indecision, and political miscalculation

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Calonne's financial administration and ministerial fall» as explicitly named facet(s) under Calonne's borrowing, spending, loss of confidence, and dismissal. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Calonne's financial administration and ministerial fall
mapping_rows.old_meaning: Calonne sustained borrowing through favorable terms, court support, and expansive spending, but worsening deficits, doubts about his credibility, political enemies, and mishandling of the Notables ended his ministry.
mapping_rows.old_stance: Distinguish his pre-reform financial management from the content of his later reform plan; the source criticizes his credit strategy and politics while acknowledging the breadth of his eventual proposals.
successor_labels: Calonne's borrowing, spending, loss of confidence, and dismissal

mapping_rows.rationale: Retain the distinct requirement «Anglo-French rivalry after the Seven Years War» as explicitly named facet(s) under American War of Independence: French intervention and fiscal consequences. Preserve its stated qualification and access; do not create another independently weighted version of the same treatment.
mapping_rows.old_label: Anglo-French rivalry after the Seven Years War
mapping_rows.old_meaning: The desire to reverse the humiliation of the Seven Years War and weaken Britain's imperial power supplied the strategic and emotional setting for French intervention in America.

evidence.old_evidence_summary: The chapter links the 1778 alliance and five-year war to restored French prestige but also to near exhaustion of the state treasury.
Necker is shown financing the American conflict mainly through loans rather than new direct taxes.
The total war cost is placed above one billion livres, with taxes and borrowing continuing after peace.
The commercial treaty is presented as a market-opening measure expected to assist French agriculture.
French hopes of avenging earlier defeat and humiliating Britain frame the decision to aid and ally with the American colonies.
Brienne announces a 1 May 1789 meeting date after the treasury is denied further advances, but the markets do not respond.
Calonne chooses a nominated assembly as a controllable display of national endorsement, but its composition and political interests make it far less compliant than he expects.
The Notables accept many general reforms while challenging the land tax, provincial representation, and the credibility of Calonne's financial claims.
Demands for accounts and doubts about the Assembly's authority lead members to argue that only the Estates-General can approve taxation.
Calonne's attempt to mobilize public pressure against the Notables fails and contributes to his dismissal.
The Assembly's demand for reliable accounts and independent auditing survives ministerial changes and ends constructive cooperation.
The narrative identifies the Assembly as the turning point that publicized the fiscal emergency and undermined confidence in absolute monarchy.
The clerical assembly grants little money and petitions for an immediate Estates-General followed by regular meetings.
Political defiance, tax arrears, harvest damage, and financier reluctance leave the government unable to obtain the advances required by its budget.
Payment suspension, compulsory government paper, financial panic, Brienne's resignation, and the loss of all reform programs mark a combined financial and political collapse.
Breton nobles authorize a deputation to accuse ministers; royal authorities arrest the delegates en route and imprison them in the Bastille.
Brienne offers full accounts, major economies, existing taxes levied more equitably, and withdrawal of the disputed imposts in exchange for registration and recall.
The plan adds staged loans, debt redemption, reduced advances, administrative centralization, and an Estates-General after projected recovery.
Brienne emerges from the Notables as the plausible successor capable of carrying reform forward.
He modifies the land tax and provincial assemblies, accepts the idea of audit, and ends the Assembly when royal prerogative blocks agreement.
He continues a reform program amid debt redemptions and worsening international pressure.
Brienne negotiates the Troyes compromise and substitutes a five-year recovery plan for the rejected new taxes.
He promises a future Estates-General, new loans, economies, and a more centralized treasury while remaining confident the program can work.
With Lamoignon he attempts to secure reform through a new judicial order and public-facing concessions.
His effort to divide opponents and manage the future Estates-General fails while tax disorder and lender distrust empty the treasury.
After payment suspension he secures Necker's return and resigns, ending the last comprehensive ministerial effort to preserve the old regime.
A newly published financial account is used to reassure readers that reform is underway before the judicial coup.
Its budget assumptions fail to account for the tax arrears and fiscal disruption created by political conflict and policy reversals.
Calonne shifts from private pressure to publication of the Assembly's proceedings and his reform proposals.
The appeal casts privileged opponents as resisting fair burdens, but public distrust makes it fail and Calonne is dismissed soon afterward.
Calonne arrives with strong court connections, favors expansive spending as a support for credit, and borrows heavily until confidence weakens.
He reveals a large deficit and argues that ordinary taxation, borrowing, and economy are no longer sufficient.
His assumption that a handpicked assembly will endorse reform exposes limited political management skills.
Enemies, distrust of his spending, and the remembered Necker surplus deprive his fiscal claims of credibility.
His handling of accounts and attempts to pressure the Notables intensify scrutiny and public attacks.
The public appeal fails, political rivals close in, and the king dismisses a minister no longer able to carry reform.
Calonne presents Louis XVI with what the narrative describes as the monarchy's most comprehensive reform proposal to date.
The plan combines a tax without privileged exemptions, provincial representation, additional revenue measures, and market-oriented economic reforms.
Its third element seeks representative endorsement to rebuild confidence and enable further borrowing.
Brienne adopts modified versions of the land tax, provincial assemblies, and other elements after Calonne falls.
Brienne plans to reduce private financial intermediation and centralize operations in a single bureaucratic treasury.
Financiers facing eventual exclusion from their traditional role are especially unwilling to provide the advances needed to bridge the crisis.
The civil-rights edict is timed to the Royal Session and to the arrival of Protestant refugees from the Dutch conflict.
The Parlement delays registration during its wider confrontation but finally registers the edict in January 1788.
Provincial nobles organize unauthorized assemblies and deputations, while clergy offer little financial support and demand immediate, regular Estates-General.
Calonne's earlier pressure on clerical contributions and Brienne's influence shape the clerical contingent's response.
Bishops oppose debt redemption because it would remove the strongest guarantee of clerical self-taxation and claim they lack authority without their own assembly.
The nominated body includes princes, prelates, nobles, magistrates, administrators, provincial estate representatives, and civic dignitaries but very few commoners.
Members' institutional loyalties, personal rivalries, and social interests shape their reception of the program.
Many members explicitly deny that they represent the nation or possess authority to approve taxation.
The queen and court favorites support Calonne's rivals, while Vergennes's patronage temporarily protects him.
Personal enemies, alienated clergy, rival ministers, Necker's admirers, and Brienne's ambitions are all represented among or around the Notables.
Courtiers, rivals, and ambitious successors exploit the failure of Calonne's public campaign until the king dismisses him.
Measures addressing criminal-law abuses and recent miscarriages of justice precede the contentious institutional reforms to attract reform-minded support.
The jurists advising on criminal reform resign in response to the wider judicial settlement, undermining the intended coalition.
The Parlement of Paris demands accounts, denies its ability to sanction permanent taxes, and invokes the Estates-General while rejecting key tax edicts.
The court repudiates forced registration and is exiled to Troyes as the government suppresses associated political activity.
Brienne negotiates a compromise that recalls the court and substitutes prolonged existing taxes for the rejected new imposts.
The Royal Session dispute opens direct conflict between court and ministry and spreads resistance among provincial parlements.
The Parlement of Paris articulates fundamental laws and binds itself against measures threatening its powers.
Arrests and the May edicts attempt to end the courts' registration and remonstrance powers through institutional reconstruction.
Provincial courts defy closure, renew demands for the Estates-General, and draw popular support against the new order.
He supports the loan program while demanding that the Estates-General meet in 1789.
His motion leads to the fundamental-laws declaration, after which the king orders his arrest and he takes refuge with the court.
He and Montsabert surrender only after an overnight confrontation and military encirclement.
Grenoble crowds resist the attempted exile of magistrates, bombard troops from roofs, and leave several dead and many injured in the event later named the Day of Tiles.
The 1786 fiscal diagnosis quantifies a severe deficit, high debt service, upcoming redemptions, and exceptional advances against future revenue.
Brienne's planned loans are intended to redeem short-term debts and reduce dependence on advances over five years.
The 1788 budget depends on a very large volume of anticipations that becomes doubtful as tax arrears and harvest damage undermine expected receipts.
When no one will provide additional anticipations, the treasury cannot continue normal payments.
Orleans objects that ordered registration is unlawful; the king's assertion of personal will alienates the court and turns the session into a constitutional disaster.
Support for the Dutch Patriots creates the prospect of costly military intervention while the budget crisis remains unresolved.
Prussian forces, encouraged by Britain, overrun the Dutch Republic while French intervention is publicly expected.
France admits it cannot intervene because financial crisis prevented preparations, exposing weakness and reducing prestige.
Calonne adopts market-oriented proposals intended to increase prosperity and ultimately improve the tax base.
Free grain trade and commutation of the corvee pass the Parlement of Paris without the confrontation generated by new taxes.
The loan plan promises rationalization of the royal household, armed forces, and financial bureaucracy.
Cuts and disbandments disrupt military careers and help explain reported officer hostility and reluctance during unrest.
Calonne considers the Estates-General as a forum for national endorsement but rejects it as too unpredictable.
Members of the Notables begin asserting that only the Estates-General can authorize new taxation.
The demand becomes general within the Assembly after the king rejects permanent independent auditing.
The Assembly bequeaths a popular call for the Estates-General to later opponents of the government.
The Parlement of Paris invokes the Estates-General when refusing stamp duty and the territorial tax.
Even the negotiated tax compromise retains the court's claim that new taxation requires national consent.
Brienne incorporates an Estates-General promised for 1792 into his five-year recovery plan.
Provincial parlements join demands for an immediate meeting as the dispute broadens.
The Parlement of Paris places regularly convoked Estates-General within its declaration of the realm's fundamental laws.
Provincial courts, nobles, and clergy all demand national or provincial Estates during resistance to the May reforms.
Brienne solicits proposals for the body's constitution partly to divide and redirect opposition.
With credit exhausted, Brienne announces 1 May 1789 for the meeting, and Necker returns as a caretaker until it convenes.
The court complies with exile to Troyes while public protests, repression, and provincial solidarity widen the dispute.
Brienne recalls the court after it accepts prolonged existing taxes, but the compromise is widely viewed as a retreat from principle.
Necker's selective public balance sheet establishes the political importance and danger of financial disclosure.
Notables distrust an unsubstantiated deficit claim in light of Necker's earlier reported surplus.
Disclosure of estimates and attack on the earlier accounts lead members to request still more detailed financial evidence.
The Notables seek a permanent auditing commission, but Louis XVI rejects it as an intrusion on prerogative.
The Parlement of Paris demands accounts before registering tax increases.
Brienne responds by promising accounts and economies within a five-year recovery plan.
A new official account is published to persuade the public that reform is succeeding before the May judicial changes.
Secret aid, naval preparation, the 1778 alliance, and five years of war are traced from the aim of weakening Britain to restored French prestige.
Brienne requests proposals and historical precedents for constituting the Estates-General, but hostile pamphleteering continues and broad design debate remains limited until the ministry falls.
Joly de Fleury raises taxation over parlementary objections and uses the revenue to support additional loans.
A third vingtieme continues after the war, while borrowing remains necessary under the next minister.

evidence.old_evidence_summary: Vergennes secured intervention, leading from secret aid in 1776 to alliance and war; restored prestige came at the cost of near financial exhaustion.
Necker financed the war almost entirely through loans while avoiding new direct taxation.
The war cost France more than 1,066 million livres, and its tax and borrowing consequences continued after peace.
Necker's system made public confidence the basis for borrowing extraordinary war expenditure.
Calonne reported a 112-million-livre deficit, debt service absorbing nearly half of revenue, and more than half the next year's income already anticipated.
Tax arrears, market nervousness, the harvest shock, and financiers' reluctance made the 1788 anticipation requirement untenable.
The treasury suspended payments after further anticipations failed, producing bankruptcy and a collapse of political authority.
Calonne presented Louis XVI with an unprecedented reform plan after years of borrowing and declining confidence.
The plan combined uniform taxation and administration, economic liberalization, and further loans sustained by public confidence.
Calonne chose a handpicked Assembly of Notables rather than the unpredictable Estates-General to confer national legitimacy on the program.
The Notables broadly accepted most proposals but challenged key tax and representation provisions and Calonne's credibility.
The Assembly's elite composition did not make it docile; Calonne misjudged both the forces released and the management of deliberation.
The Notables demanded full accounts, disputed their representative authority, and heard the first explicit claim that only the Estates-General could approve taxation.
Under Brienne they continued to demand authoritative fiscal scrutiny and ended constructive work after the king vetoed a permanent audit commission.
The Assembly publicized the monarchy's financial incapacity, encouraged resistance, and made the Estates-General a popular constitutional demand.
Leaks from the nominally secret Assembly fueled hostile pamphleteering and shaped the Notables' demand for accounts.
Calonne's published appeal against privilege failed to mobilize opinion and instead appeared a desperate maneuver.
The Assembly involved public opinion in politics on a sustained scale and left opponents expecting resolute resistance from the parlements.
Crowds, salons, political clubs, and a rapidly growing pamphlet press openly backed parliamentary opposition to the tax edicts.
Brienne's effort to redirect debate toward the form of the Estates-General did little to stem hundreds of hostile pamphlets.
The parlement refused the stamp and territorial taxes without accounts and declared that only the Estates-General could sanction them.
It declared forced registration illegal, pursued Calonne, and was exiled to Troyes amid public disorder.
Brienne secured its return through a compromise replacing new taxes with prolonged vingtièmes, provoking skepticism and provincial resentment.
After the Royal Session the parlement dissociated itself from forced loan registration and escalated attacks on arbitrary royal authority.
A Notable first asserted that taxation belonged only to the Estates-General.
Calls for a truly national assembly became universal within the Notables and helped end their session.
The parlement of Paris grounded its rejection of new taxes in the exclusive authority of the Estates-General.
Brienne incorporated a meeting by 1792 into his finance plan to secure parliamentary support.
The parlement's declaration of fundamental laws included the nation's right to grant subsidies through a regularly convoked Estates-General.
Brienne set 1 May 1789 as the meeting date in a failed attempt to revive credit immediately before the payment suspension.
The reforms transferred registration and remonstrance to a Plenary Court, curtailed parlementary jurisdiction, and suppressed offices.
Courts, lawyers, crowds, nobles, clergy, and provincial institutions resisted, producing riots, exiles, and administrative paralysis.
The ministry's attempt to divide opposition through debate over the future Estates-General failed to displace hostility to the judicial reforms.
The treasury was empty and financiers would accept no further anticipations after months of fiscal disorder and resistance.
Payment suspension on 16 August triggered market panic, Brienne's resignation, and Necker's return.
The author concludes that the monarchy's bankruptcy was financial, political, and intellectual, leaving a vacuum of power.
Turgot warned that the first gunshot would drive the State to bankruptcy and that intervention would destroy prospects for financial reform.
Necker raised 520 million livres in loans, published a selective ordinary-account surplus, and won strong public confidence before resigning.
The Notables measured Calonne's deficit against the remembered Compte rendu and Necker's public reputation.
Calonne's attack on the Compte rendu intensified demands for detailed accounts and divided those uncertain whom to believe.
Necker's unmatched credit and public prestige made his recall the last available means of calming the bankruptcy crisis.
Calonne borrowed more than 653 million livres while defending lavish 'useful splendour,' before loan subscriptions and political support weakened.
Notables distrusted his deficit claim because of his notorious spending and borrowing and their memory of Necker's reported surplus.
His attempt to mobilize public pressure against the Notables failed, and Louis XVI dismissed him on 8 April 1787.
The proposal abolished exemptions and substituted a permanent tax in kind on all landowners, assessed through provincial assemblies.
The Notables accepted tax equality but questioned a perpetual variable land tax, payment in kind, and estate representation.
Clerical objections tied reform to the Church's corporate debt and traditional self-taxation.
The parlement rejected the territorial tax and asserted that only the Estates-General could authorize it.
Calonne proposed assemblies of taxpayers to assess and administer the territorial subvention with intendants.
The Notables demanded guaranteed clerical and noble seats and questioned intendants' veto power.
Bordeaux withheld registration because assembly powers were vague, although Paris registered the edict.
Experience with nominated assemblies and punitive tax assessments strengthened demands for provincial estates with broader constituencies and stronger powers.
Calonne, advised by Dupont de Nemours, revived grain, customs, corvée, and commercial-treaty measures intended to stimulate prosperity.
Free grain trade and corvée commutation were registered with little resistance before the taxation battle.
Brienne took control of finance, modified the territorial tax and assemblies, but could not overcome demands for audited accounts.
He pressed forward after the Notables despite debt redemptions and worsening international pressures.
His five-year plan exchanged new taxes for prolonged vingtièmes, promised accounts and economies, and used negotiation to recover the parlement's cooperation.
The plan relied on large loans, reduced anticipations, administrative centralization, and a promised Estates-General by 1792.
After payment suspension he obtained Necker's return and resigned, ending the last ministerial effort to preserve the old regime.
Brienne convened an unprecedented Royal Session to gain authoritative registration of 420 million livres in loans.
Louis XVI's declaration that registration was legal because he wished it transformed a probable victory into a constitutional confrontation.

after.meaning: Lower courts, the Paris bar, reform jurists, and provincial tribunals refused to recognize or cooperate with the new judicial order, bringing ordinary justice close to a standstill.
after.qualification: Preserve the limited exceptions: some lower courts were tempted by promotion, but uncertainty and institutional loyalties prevented broad compliance.

after.meaning: Unauthorized noble assemblies and the Assembly of the Clergy joined demands for national or provincial Estates and denounced ministerial policy, broadening resistance beyond magistrates and crowds.
after.qualification: Keep noble and clerical motives distinct even when providing a shared route to the cross-estate coalition; neither group should be presented as speaking for all commoners or all France.

after.meaning: Although troops enforced some arrests and registrations, officers whose careers had been harmed by reforms were widely suspected of hostility, and commanders hesitated to use lethal force against rioters.
after.qualification: Do not claim military mutiny: the source explicitly notes that no officer disobeyed a decisive order, while emphasizing reluctance and political unreliability.

after.meaning: The Crown used large numbers of royal warrants to silence and remove magistrates at Toulouse, Besancon, Dijon, Metz, Rouen, and other centers after courts defied the May settlement.
after.qualification: Treat the exiles as a coordinated coercive response that widened resistance, not merely as a list of local punishments.

after.meaning: At Pau, a crowd broke into the locked courthouse and physically restored the magistrates, directly reversing royal enforcement of the May settlement.

after.meaning: At Rennes, law clerks, students, and urban workers dominated the streets for weeks and expelled the intendant, exposing disagreement and hesitation within local command.

after.meaning: The clergy's representative assembly offered a very small voluntary grant and joined calls for immediate and regularly recurring Estates-General despite Brienne's clerical status.
after.qualification: Treat the episode as institutional clerical opposition and a significant loss of support for the ministry, not as evidence that all clergy held one political position.

after.meaning: Breton nobles organized unauthorized resistance, denounced ministers, and sent deputies toward Versailles, where the delegates were arrested and imprisoned in the Bastille.
after.qualification: Preserve the source's label of noble revolt and the corporate nature of the action; do not convert it into a generalized popular movement.
